_readme: Today in Catholic History. Keys are MM-DD; each holds one or more events.
This file grows over time: a scheduled research agent fills in dates that
have no entry yet (see scripts/history-agent-brief.md). It is safe to edit
by hand — keep keys zero-padded, keep years as numbers, and keep each text
to one or two plain sentences.
Seed entries were written from well-established dates but have not been
individually source-checked; the agent adds a `source` as it verifies them.

01-04.text: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton died at Emmitsburg, Maryland. A widow with five children who converted at 30, she went on to found the first Catholic girls' school in the United States, and became the first native-born American citizen to be canonized.

01-25.text: John XXIII announced he would convene an ecumenical council. He had been pope barely three months, and almost nobody expected it — the announcement reportedly met with silence from the cardinals in the room.

02-11.text: A 14-year-old named Bernadette Soubirous saw a woman in a grotto outside Lourdes while gathering firewood. Her family was so poor they were living in a former jail cell.
Benedict XVI announced his resignation, in Latin, at a routine consistory. He was the first pope to step down voluntarily in nearly six centuries.

03-07.text: St. Thomas Aquinas died at Fossanova on his way to the Council of Lyon. He had stopped writing months earlier, saying that after what he had seen in prayer, everything he had written seemed like straw.

03-13.text: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was elected pope and took the name Francis — the first pope from the Americas, the first Jesuit, and the first to take that name.

03-24.text: St. Óscar Romero was shot dead while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel in San Salvador, one day after publicly calling on soldiers to stop carrying out the government's killings.

04-02.text: Pope St. John Paul II died in the Apostolic Palace after 26 years as pope. Crowds had filled St. Peter's Square for days; this ministry carries his name.

04-19.text: Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger was elected on the fourth ballot and took the name Benedict XVI.

04-27.text: John XXIII and John Paul II were canonized together by Pope Francis, with Benedict XVI also present — two living popes and two new saints in one morning.

05-30.text: St. Joan of Arc was burned at the stake at Rouen, aged about 19. The Church that condemned her retried the case 25 years later and declared her innocent.

06-05.text: St. Boniface was killed in Frisia along with his companions. Accounts say he raised a book to shield himself from the sword.

06-22.text: Galileo Galilei was condemned by the Roman Inquisition and made to abjure his defence of a sun-centred cosmos. The Church formally acknowledged the errors of the case in 1992.

07-06.text: St. Thomas More was beheaded on Tower Hill for refusing to endorse Henry VIII's claim over the Church in England. He said he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

07-31.text: St. Ignatius of Loyola died in Rome. A soldier until a cannonball shattered his leg, he spent the long convalescence reading the only books available — the life of Christ and the lives of the saints.

08-04.text: St. John Vianney died at Ars. He had struggled badly with his studies and was nearly refused ordination; he ended up spending as much as sixteen hours a day hearing confessions.

08-14.text: St. Maximilian Kolbe died in the starvation bunker at Auschwitz. He had stepped forward to take the place of a stranger, a married man with children, who had been picked to die.

08-28.text: St. Augustine died at Hippo while the city was under siege. His Confessions is still, sixteen centuries on, one of the most honest books ever written about wanting to be good and not managing it.

09-04.text: Mother Teresa of Calcutta was canonized in St. Peter's Square.

09-05.text: St. Teresa of Calcutta died. Her private letters, published later, revealed decades of interior darkness she had kept almost entirely to herself.

09-23.text: St. Padre Pio died at San Giovanni Rotondo.

09-27.text: St. Vincent de Paul died in Paris at 80. He later wrote that Barbary pirates had captured him at sea in 1605 and sold him into slavery in Tunis — a story known only from his own letters — before he escaped and spent his life organising care for foundlings, galley slaves, and the rural poor.

09-30.text: St. Thérèse of Lisieux died of tuberculosis at 24, having spent nine years in a Carmelite convent and done nothing the world would call remarkable. She is now a Doctor of the Church.

10-03.text: St. Francis of Assisi died on the evening of 3 October at the Portiuncula, having asked to be laid on the bare ground.

10-05.text: St. Faustina Kowalska died of tuberculosis in Kraków at 33. A former domestic servant with no formal education, she had spent her years as a nun recording visions of Christ in a diary that later became the basis for the Divine Mercy devotion.

10-06.text: St. Bruno of Cologne died at Serra San Bruno in Calabria, aged about 70. He had given up a prominent teaching post at Reims to live as a hermit, and the order he founded, the Carthusians, still keeps a rule of near-total silence.

10-07.text: A fleet of the Holy League, a coalition Pope St. Pius V had organized from Spain, Venice, and the Papal States, destroyed the main Ottoman navy at Lepanto in the Gulf of Patras. Pius, who had asked Catholics across Europe to pray the rosary for the fleet, credited the victory to Mary and instituted a feast in thanksgiving.

10-11.text: The Second Vatican Council opened in St. Peter's Basilica with over 2,000 bishops present — the largest gathering of its kind in the Church's history.

10-13.text: An estimated 70,000 people gathered in a field near Fátima, Portugal, after three shepherd children said the Virgin Mary had promised a sign that day. Witnesses, including secular journalists, described the sun appearing to spin and plunge toward the crowd — an event since known as the Miracle of the Sun.

10-15.text: St. Teresa of Ávila, a Carmelite nun and mystic known for reforming her order and writing on prayer, died at Alba de Tormes on the very night Spain switched from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar. The reform erased October 5 through 14 that year, so she is recorded as dying on either October 4 or October 15 — the date now kept as her feast.

10-16.text: Karol Wojtyła was elected pope and took the name John Paul II — the first non-Italian in 455 years. He told the crowd he would correct himself if he made mistakes in their Italian.

10-18.text: Isaac Jogues, a French Jesuit missionary who had already survived a year of Mohawk captivity and mutilation, returned as a missionary to the Mohawk village of Ossernenon in present-day New York and was killed with a tomahawk, then beheaded. He is venerated as one of the eight North American Martyrs.

10-19.text: Pope John Paul II beatified Mother Teresa of Calcutta, the Albanian-born nun known for her work with the destitute and dying in India, before a crowd estimated at 300,000 in St. Peter's Square — just six years after her death in 1997.

10-21.text: St. Kateri Tekakwitha was canonized, the first Native American saint. She was orphaned by smallpox at four and left badly scarred by it.

10-22.text: John Paul II celebrated the Mass inaugurating his pontificate in St. Peter's Square, telling the crowd in his homily, "Do not be afraid! Open wide the doors for Christ." The phrase became a hallmark of his 26-year papacy.

10-23.text: St. John of Capistrano, a Franciscan friar who had helped recruit and lead the peasant army that broke the Ottoman siege of Belgrade, died three months later at Ilok, in present-day Croatia, worn down from tending the siege's wounded and plague-stricken survivors. He was 70.

10-24.text: St. Anthony Mary Claret, founder of the Claretian missionaries and former confessor to Queen Isabella II of Spain, died at Fontfroide Abbey in France. He had followed the deposed queen into exile and spent his final months there under house arrest at the insistence of the Spanish government.

10-27.text: Pope John Paul II convened a World Day of Prayer for Peace at Assisi, inviting leaders of thirteen world religions to the hometown of St. Francis. Each tradition prayed separately, in its own space, rather than together, so the event would not look like all faiths being merged into one.

10-28.text: The Second Vatican Council promulgated Nostra Aetate, its declaration on relations with non-Christian religions, which repudiated antisemitism and reframed the Church's stance toward Judaism and other world religions.

10-31.text: Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and theology professor at Wittenberg, circulated his Ninety-Five Theses attacking the sale of indulgences; the familiar story that he nailed them to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church is a later tradition, not a contemporary record. The dispute he opened grew into the Protestant Reformation and the Western Church's permanent division.

11-01.text: Pius XII defined the Assumption of Mary as dogma in Munificentissimus Deus — the only time a pope has explicitly invoked papal infallibility since it was defined in 1870.

11-02.text: Odilo, abbot of the French monastery of Cluny, decreed that all its houses keep November 2 as a day of prayer for the souls of the dead — the origin of All Souls' Day. The custom then spread through the rest of the Western Church over the next three centuries.

11-03.text: St. Charles Borromeo died at Milan, aged 46. He had stayed in the city through the plague of 1576 when much of the civil government left.

11-07.text: St. Willibrord, an Anglo-Saxon monk sent from England to evangelize the pagan Frisians of the Low Countries, died at about 81 at the monastery he had founded at Echternach, in present-day Luxembourg. He is remembered as the Apostle to the Frisians.

11-08.text: St. Martin of Tours, a former Roman soldier who became a monk and then bishop after reportedly cutting his cloak in half to clothe a beggar, died at Candes in Gaul. His feast is kept three days later, on the date of his burial at Tours rather than his death.

11-09.text: Pope St. Sylvester I dedicated the Lateran Basilica in Rome, the first public Christian church built in the city. It remains the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, a rank that technically outranks St. Peter's Basilica.

11-10.text: Pope St. Leo the Great died in Rome after more than two decades as pope. He is best remembered for persuading Attila the Hun to turn back from invading Italy in 452, and for a theological letter, the Tome of Leo, that shaped the Council of Chalcedon's teaching on Christ's two natures.

11-12.text: St. Josaphat Kuncevych, an Eastern Catholic archbishop working to bring Ruthenian Christians into union with Rome, was killed by an Orthodox mob in Vitebsk that opposed the union. He was struck down with an axe and his body thrown into a river; he later became the first Eastern-rite saint canonized by Rome.

11-13.text: Pope St. Nicholas I died in Rome after nine years as pope, during which he excommunicated the archbishop of Ravenna for abusing his authority and forced the bishops who had sanctioned King Lothair II's attempted divorce to recant. Later historians nicknamed him "the Great" for asserting papal authority over kings and bishops alike.

11-15.text: St. Albert the Great, a Dominican friar who taught Thomas Aquinas and wrote on nearly every branch of learning known in his day, died at Cologne. He is now the Church's patron saint of natural scientists.

11-16.text: Six Jesuit priests and two women were shot dead by an army unit on the campus of the Jesuit-run University of Central America in San Salvador, during El Salvador's civil war. The priests, including the university's rector Ignacio Ellacuría, had been outspoken advocates for a negotiated end to the war.

11-17.text: St. Elizabeth of Hungary died at Marburg at 24. After her husband's death four years earlier, she gave up her position as a noblewoman, built a hospital below the Wartburg castle, and spent her remaining years caring for the sick and poor.

11-18.text: Pope Urban VIII dedicated the newly completed St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, 120 years after construction began under Pope Julius II. The current basilica replaced a fourth-century church built over the traditional site of St. Peter's tomb.

11-20.text: Edmund, the Anglo-Saxon king of East Anglia, was killed by the Viking army that had already conquered much of eastern England. He was venerated as a martyr soon afterward, though the detailed stories of his death — not written down until more than a century later — are considered legendary rather than documented history.

11-21.text: The Second Vatican Council promulgated Lumen Gentium, its dogmatic constitution on the nature of the Church, after a vote of 2,151 to 5 among the assembled bishops.

11-27.text: Catherine Labouré, a French novice with the Daughters of Charity, reported seeing the Virgin Mary in her convent's chapel on Paris's Rue du Bac and was shown the design for what became the Miraculous Medal. It was the second of three apparitions she described that year.

11-28.text: St. James of the Marches, a Franciscan preacher and one of the leading figures of the Observant reform movement alongside St. John of Capistrano, died in Naples in his eighties. He had also founded early nonprofit pawnshops, called montes pietatis, to lend to the poor without the high rates charged by private moneylenders.

12-01.text: Charles de Foucauld, a French hermit who had lived for years among the Tuareg people in the Algerian Sahara, was shot dead by raiders at his hermitage in Tamanrasset. He left no followers in his own lifetime, but the religious communities inspired by his writings were founded decades after his death.

12-03.text: St. Francis Xavier died on Shangchuan Island, within sight of mainland China, which he had spent his last months trying to enter.

12-04.text: The Second Vatican Council's first two completed documents, the constitution on the liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium) and the decree on media (Inter Mirifica), were promulgated by Pope Paul VI. Sacrosanctum Concilium's call to reform worship led directly to the Mass being said in local languages instead of Latin.

12-05.text: Pope Innocent VIII issued the bull Summis Desiderantes Affectibus, authorizing two Dominican friars, Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger, to prosecute witchcraft in parts of Germany. Kramer printed the bull as a preface to his own witch-hunting manual, the Malleus Maleficarum, to borrow its authority.

12-07.text: Ambrose, the Roman governor of Milan, was consecrated bishop of the city just eight days after his baptism, after a crowd spontaneously called for him to fill the vacant post while he was still only a catechumen preparing for baptism. His actual death came nearly 23 years later, on April 4, 397.

12-08.text: Pius IX defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus.
The Second Vatican Council formally closed, just over three years after it opened.

12-09.text: According to a tradition first set down in writing in 1649, more than a century after the fact, a farmer named Juan Diego met a young woman on Tepeyac hill outside Mexico City who spoke to him in his own Nahuatl language. No document naming Juan Diego survives from before that account, and historians still debate how much of the story can be verified.

12-10.text: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize medal and diploma at a ceremony in the Aula of the University of Oslo, more than six weeks after the Norwegian Nobel Committee's October 27 announcement of the award.

12-11.text: Pope St. Damasus I died in Rome after eighteen years as pope, during which he commissioned the scholar Jerome to produce a single standardized Latin translation of the Bible — the work that became known as the Vulgate.

12-13.text: The Council of Trent opened. It ran on and off for eighteen years and shaped Catholic life for the four centuries that followed.

12-14.text: St. John of the Cross, a Spanish Carmelite friar and mystical writer, died at a monastery in Úbeda at 49. Fellow Carmelites opposed to his reform efforts had imprisoned him in a cramped cell in Toledo years earlier, and he composed some of his best-known poetry there before escaping after nine months.

12-16.text: Bl. Honorat Koźmiński, a Polish Capuchin friar, died at Nowe Miasto at 87. After Russian authorities suppressed religious orders in Poland following the failed 1864 uprising, he responded by founding numerous religious congregations whose members took vows in secret, wearing no habit and living outside any community, to evade the ban.

12-25.text: Charlemagne was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in St. Peter's during Christmas Mass — a moment that set the terms of the relationship between Church and European rulers for centuries.

12-29.text: St. Thomas Becket was killed by four knights in his own cathedral at Canterbury, after Henry II reportedly wondered aloud who would rid him of the troublesome priest.
